fact: Computers operate on binary values as a result of being built from transistors, and there are 4 commonly known integer representations: unsigned, sign magnitude, one's complement and two's complement
Virtually all modern computers operate based on 2's complement representation, for two reasons: the hardware is faster, and the hardware is simpler, which makes it faster
The standard binary encoding, unsigned, gives only positive values, with a range of 0 to 2 to the power n minus 1 for n bits
For 4 bits the unsigned values run 0 to 15, since 2 to the power 4 minus 1 is 15
In the 4-bit table binary 1010 is decimal 10 and hex a, 1100 is decimal 12 and hex c, and 1111 is decimal 15 and hex f
Negative numbers are essential, and any computer not capable of dealing with them would not be particularly useful
The methods used to represent negative numbers in binary are the sign-magnitude method, one's complement and two's complement

Sign magnitude uses 1 bit of the integer to represent the sign, with a sign bit of 0 for positive and 1 for negative, and the rest of the integer is a magnitude using the same encoding as unsigned integers
The hardware that does arithmetic on sign magnitude integers is not fast, and it is more complex than the hardware that does arithmetic on 1's complement and 2's complement integers

The class exercise asks for 74 and minus 43 in an 8-bit register in sign-magnitude, and the method given is to find the positive value in binary first and then flip the sign bit, as the worked line minus 38 equals 10100110 shows
In 4-bit sign magnitude 0101 is 5 and 1101 is minus 5, and to get the additive inverse of a number you just flip the sign bit
The sign magnitude range is minus 2 to the power n minus 1, plus 1, up to 2 to the power n minus 1, minus 1, so with 4 bits it runs from minus 7 to plus 7

Because of the sign bit there are 2 representations for 0 in sign magnitude, 0000 and 1000, which is a problem for hardware since the computer must make all calculations come out the same whichever representation is used
Sign reversal and absolute value operations are easy using sign-magnitude representation
Adding the negative of a number is not the same as subtraction in sign-magnitude, so different operations must be defined for addition and subtraction with sign-magnitude numbers
The ones' complement form of a negative binary number is the bitwise NOT applied to its positive counterpart, so negation is done by taking a bitwise complement of the positive representation
Like sign-and-magnitude, ones' complement has two representations of 0: 00000000 for plus 0 and 11111111 for minus 0, and positive integers use the same representation as unsigned
The ones' complement form of 00101011, which is 43, becomes 11010100, which is minus 43
The 1's complement value 11100 must be negative, and since its additive inverse 00011 is plus 3 by sight, 11100 must be minus 3

The range of signed numbers using ones' complement is minus 2 to the power N minus 1, minus 1, up to 2 to the power N minus 1, minus 1, plus and minus zero, so a conventional 8-bit range is minus 127 to plus 127
To add two numbers in ones' complement you do a conventional binary addition and then an end-around carry, that is, add any resulting carry back into the resulting sum
The end-around carry is demonstrated by adding minus 1, which is 11111110, to plus 2, which is 00000010
In that example the binary addition alone gives 00000000, which is incorrect, and only when the carry is added back in does the correct result 00000001 appear
The ones' complement numeric representation system was common in older computers like the PDP-1, the CDC 160 series and the UNIVAC 1100/2200 series

The system is referred to as ones' complement because the negation of a positive value x can also be formed by subtracting x from the ones' complement representation of zero, which is a long sequence of ones, that is minus 0
The ones' complement representation of a negative number can be obtained from the sign-magnitude representation merely by bitwise complementing the magnitude
Two's complement solves the problems of multiple representations of 0 and the need for the end-around carry
In 2's complement, negative numbers are represented by the bit pattern which is one greater, in an unsigned sense, than the ones' complement of the positive value

The quick method for a two's complement is to write down the positive binary number, copy the digits from the right hand side up to and including the first 1, then invert the rest, so 14 as 001110 becomes 110010 for minus 14 in 6 bits
In 8-bit two's complement, plus 24 is 00011000, plus 127 is 01111111, minus 39 is 11011001, minus 92 is 10100100 and minus 128 is 10000000
The two's complement 110011 must be negative since the most significant bit is a 1, and taking its 1's complement gives 001100, adding 1 gives 001101 which is plus 13, so 110011 is minus 13

The mid-lecture quiz asks students to describe how negative integers are formed using sign-magnitude, 1's and 2's complement, to say what 111100111 represents in each, and to perform 47 plus 35 in 2's complement using 6 bits and state what value would be stored in the register
When a value cannot be represented in the number of bits allowed or specified we say that an overflow has occurred, and overflow occurs when doing arithmetic operations
For unsigned in 3 bits, 8 would require at least 4 bits, that is 1000, and for sign-magnitude in 4 bits, 8 would require at least 5 bits, that is 01000
In the 3-bit unsigned overflow example 011, which is 3, plus 110, which is 6, gives 1 001, which is 9, and 9 would require 4 bits, so the addition overflows

The homework asks for minus 89 in sign-magnitude, 1's and 2's complement using an 8-bit register, the range of a 16-bit register under sign-magnitude, the value of 10111011 in all three systems, and 23.5 in IEEE single precision expressed in hexadecimal

The revision class groups data representation as unsigned numbers, signed numbers, which are sign-magnitude, 1's complement with end-around carry and 2's complement, and other representations, which are floating point numbers and graphics and objects
In the spacecraft telemetry question a 16-bit processor using 2's complement must store Temperature of minus 182, Pressure of 487 and Altitude of minus 1023

The telemetry question asks for the range of a 16-bit two's complement system, whether the given numbers fall within it, each value in binary and hexadecimal, and a demonstration of minus 182 plus 487
For a 16-bit two's complement system the range is minus 2 to the power 15 up to 2 to the power 15 minus 1, that is minus 32768 to 32767, and all three telemetry values fall within the range
Minus 182 is worked as plus 182 in 16 bits, 0000000010110110, inverted to 1111111101001001 for the 1's complement, plus 1 to give 1111111101001010, which is hex FF4A
Pressure 487 in 16-bit binary is 0000000111100111, which is hex 01E7
Minus 1023 is worked as plus 1023, 0000001111111111, inverted to 1111110000000000, plus 1, giving hex FC01, although the slide prints the sum with one digit too many
